I'm fifty-five years old, and I've worked these fields in Quzhou County since I was a teenager. I finished middle school, so I can read the seed labels and do my accounts, but the real knowledge is in my hands and in what I've watched my neighbors do year after year. It's early April now, and my winter wheat is already in the ground—I sowed it last October, the way my father did and the way everyone around here does.

I have eight mu of flat, irrigated land, and I'm not going to gamble with it. Some people talk about growing vegetables or cotton when prices look good, but one bad rain or one bad price and you lose your whole year. Wheat and maize may not make you rich, but they don't make you poor either. That's the rotation I've always done, and that's what I'll stick to.

My wheat is already growing. I used an improved variety—shimai or liangxing, the kind you buy from the supply shop that yields better than the old traditional seeds but doesn't cost like fancy foreign seed. After the wheat comes off in early June, I'll plant summer maize the same day or the next day. Time is short before frost, so I use hybrid seed—NK815 or nongda372, one small bag per mu. I don't till before the maize; there's no time and it wastes diesel. I drill it straight into the wheat stubble.

For fertilizer, I know what this soil needs. I'll put down compound fertilizer as a base and top up with urea at the key growth stages. The wheat needs more phosphorus up front, so the compound for wheat is heavier in P. The maize needs nitrogen for the big ear, so I make sure it gets enough. Water is everything here—we pump from wells. I'll irrigate the wheat four times: winter storage water if it's dry, then green-up, jointing, and heading. The maize only needs two good irrigations, one at sowing if June is dry and one at the big ear stage. As for pests, they come every year like clockwork. I'll spray the wheat four times—herbicide early, then insecticide twice, and fungicide once at heading. The maize gets three sprays.

My neighbors and I all farm more or less the same way. If it was good enough for my father and it's good enough for the people I trust, it's good enough for me.
